title: Alcohol-Free NyQuil and Cold Medicine: What's Safe and What Isn't
excerpt: Is there an alcohol-free NyQuil? A lookup table of alcohol-free cold, cough and sleep medicines, how much alcohol regular NyQuil has, and why alcohol-free doesn't mean safe with drinks.
metaDescription: Is there an alcohol-free NyQuil? Which cold, cough and sleep medicines are alcohol-free, how much alcohol NyQuil has, and why it still clashes with drinks.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, there is an alcohol-free NyQuil, and most of the cold, cough and sleep medicines you'll find on a US pharmacy shelf today are made without alcohol. Vicks sells a version labeled "Alcohol Free" next to the original NyQuil liquid, which lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient at 10%. Robitussin, ZzzQuil, Benadryl, DayQuil and nearly every tablet, caplet, softgel and LiquiCap are alcohol-free or use no drinking alcohol in the formula. But there's a catch that matters more than the bottle: **an alcohol-free medicine is not the same as a medicine that's safe to take with alcohol.** The active ingredients in NyQuil, ZzzQuil and Benadryl still clash with any drinks already in your system.

**The quick rules:** If you want to avoid alcohol in the bottle, look for "alcohol free" on the front of the box, then confirm it by reading the "Inactive ingredients" line in the Drug Facts panel. Pills, caplets and liquid-filled capsules are the easiest way to avoid it. If you've been drinking tonight, an alcohol-free product does not make it safe to take a sedating cold or sleep medicine. Wait until you're fully sober. If you take disulfiram (Antabuse) or metronidazole, or you're shopping for a child, ask a pharmacist to help you pick the product.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide explains what is printed on US over-the-counter labels and what's generally known about how these ingredients interact with alcohol. Formulas change, and store brands vary, so the label on the box in your hand is the final word. **Talk to a pharmacist or doctor before choosing a cold or sleep medicine if** you take disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole, tinidazole, a sedative, an antidepressant, an opioid, or any other prescription drug; you have liver disease, glaucoma, breathing problems such as sleep apnea, or trouble urinating from an enlarged prostate; you're pregnant or breastfeeding; or you're buying for a child. **Get help now (call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the US, or 911 in an emergency) if** someone who mixed a cold or sleep medicine with alcohol can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or is vomiting while very drowsy.

## Why "Alcohol-Free" Doesn't Mean "Safe With Alcohol"

People search for alcohol-free NyQuil for two very different reasons, and it helps to separate them.

1. **You don't want any alcohol in your medicine.** Maybe you don't drink for religious or personal reasons, you're pregnant, you're giving it to a child, you take a medicine that reacts badly to even small amounts of alcohol, or you simply want to avoid it. For you, the alcohol in the bottle is the whole question, and this guide has a product table below.
2. **You've been drinking and want something that won't "add more alcohol."** This is the more common reason, and it's where the alcohol-free label can mislead you. The alcohol inside a dose of original NyQuil is small. The real risk when you've been drinking comes from the **active ingredients**, and those are the same in the alcohol-free version.

Here's the interaction in plain words. Most night-time cold and sleep products get their drowsiness from a **sedating antihistamine**, usually doxylamine (in NyQuil) or diphenhydramine (in ZzzQuil, Benadryl and most "PM" products). These block histamine in the brain, which is one of the chemicals that keeps you awake. Alcohol is also a sedative, working through a different route: it boosts GABA, the brain's main calming signal. Put the two together and you're pressing two different brakes on the same system. The combined drowsiness, unsteadiness and slowed reactions can be much stronger than either one alone. In a person who drank heavily, that stacking can, in rare cases, slow breathing.

Two other common ingredients add their own problems:

- **Acetaminophen** (the drug in Tylenol) is in NyQuil Cold & Flu, DayQuil Cold & Flu, Theraflu and many store brands. The FDA-required liver warning says severe liver damage may occur if you take more than the daily maximum, combine it with other acetaminophen products, or have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using it. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Dextromethorphan (DXM)**, the cough suppressant in most "DM" and night-time cough products, can cause dizziness and drowsiness on its own. Alcohol makes those effects stronger.

None of that changes when the alcohol is taken out of the bottle. So the right way to read an "alcohol free" label is: *this tells me what's in the medicine, not what's already in my bloodstream.*

## How Much Alcohol Is Actually in Original NyQuil?

The original NyQuil Cold & Flu liquid lists alcohol at 10% as an inactive ingredient. It's there to help keep the active ingredients dissolved and stable, which is a common job for alcohol in liquid medicines.

To put that number in perspective, here's simple arithmetic rather than a lab measurement. An adult dose of NyQuil liquid is 30 mL (two tablespoons). Ten percent of that is about 3 mL of alcohol, which weighs roughly 2.4 grams. A US standard drink contains about 14 grams of alcohol. So one dose of original NyQuil contains something in the range of a sixth of a standard drink.

That's why the alcohol content isn't the main safety issue for most adults. It does matter for a few groups of people, though, and those are the people the alcohol-free version is mostly for.

## Who Really Needs an Alcohol-Free Cold Medicine

For most healthy adults, the small amount of alcohol in a liquid medicine isn't a medical problem. These are the situations where choosing alcohol-free is worth the extra minute at the shelf:

- **You take disulfiram (Antabuse).** Disulfiram causes a severe reaction (flushing, pounding heart, nausea, vomiting) when it meets alcohol, and its prescribing information warns people to avoid alcohol in disguised forms, including cough syrups and other liquid medicines. Even small amounts can trigger it. Ask your pharmacist to check every product you buy.
- **You take metronidazole (Flagyl) or tinidazole.** These antibiotics carry warnings to avoid alcohol during treatment and for a period afterward. Our [antibiotics and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) covers which ones carry this warning and why.
- **You're buying for a child.** Children's cold and allergy products sold in the US today are generally formulated without alcohol. Many cough and cold products are not meant for young children at all, so follow the age limits on the label and ask a pediatrician or pharmacist if you're unsure.
- **You're pregnant or breastfeeding.** The alcohol amount is small, but many people prefer to avoid it entirely. More importantly, several active ingredients in multi-symptom products aren't recommended in pregnancy without advice, so this is one to ask your doctor or pharmacist about.
- **You avoid alcohol for religious, personal or health reasons.** That's reason enough to read the label.
- **You're about to take an alcohol test.** A dose of a 10% liquid shortly before a breath test could, in theory, register mouth alcohol for a short time. Sensitive urine tests that look for alcohol breakdown products (such as EtG tests) can pick up small exposures, and US federal guidance on these tests has flagged incidental sources like medicines and mouthwash. If you're subject to testing, use an alcohol-free product and tell the tester what you've taken.

## Alcohol-Free Cold, Cough and Sleep Products: The Lookup Table

This table is a starting point, built from US product labels. It tells you whether the **formula** is generally alcohol-free and whether the **active ingredients** are a problem if you've been drinking. Brands reformulate, sizes and versions multiply, and store brands differ, so always check the "Inactive ingredients" line on your box.

| Product | Alcohol in the formula? | Main active ingredients | If you've been drinking |
|---|---|---|---|
| NyQuil Cold & Flu liquid (original) | Yes, listed at 10% | Acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, doxylamine | Avoid. Sedative stacking plus a liver load |
| NyQuil Alcohol Free Cold & Flu liquid | No, labeled "Alcohol Free" | Same three as the original | Avoid. The alcohol-free label doesn't change the interaction |
| NyQuil LiquiCaps | No drinking alcohol in the formula | Acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, doxylamine | Avoid. Same ingredients in capsule form |
| DayQuil Cold & Flu (liquid and LiquiCaps) | Generally made without alcohol | Acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, phenylephrine | Not sedating, but acetaminophen still counts toward the liver warning |
| ZzzQuil Nighttime Sleep-Aid (liquid and LiquiCaps) | Generally made without alcohol | Diphenhydramine | Avoid on a drinking night. Strong sedative stacking |
| Benadryl Allergy tablets and liqui-gels | No drinking alcohol in the formula | Diphenhydramine | Avoid on a drinking night. Same as ZzzQuil |
| Children's Benadryl liquid | Children's versions are generally made without alcohol | Diphenhydramine | Not for adults who've been drinking; follow child dosing and age limits |
| Robitussin cough liquids (most current versions) | Most current versions are made without alcohol | Varies: guaifenesin, dextromethorphan, or both | Plain guaifenesin is the mildest; DM versions add dizziness and drowsiness |
| Mucinex tablets (plain, DM, D) | No drinking alcohol in the formula | Guaifenesin, with DXM or pseudoephedrine in some | Extended-release tablets last about 12 hours, so the effects overlap with an evening of drinking |
| Delsym 12-Hour Cough liquid | Check the label | Dextromethorphan (extended release) | Long-acting DXM; adds to drowsiness and dizziness |
| Theraflu hot-drink powders | No drinking alcohol in the formula | Usually acetaminophen plus others | Acetaminophen counts toward the liver warning |
| Diabetic Tussin and similar sugar-free syrups | Marketed as alcohol-free and sugar-free | Varies by version | Depends on the active ingredients; check for DXM or antihistamines |
| Store-brand "Nighttime" liquids | Varies. Some contain alcohol, some don't | Usually copies NyQuil's three ingredients | Avoid on a drinking night |

### How to read the table

- **"No drinking alcohol in the formula"** means the product doesn't use ethanol as a solvent. Tablets, caplets and liquid-filled capsules almost never need it.
- **"Generally made without alcohol"** means current US versions we're aware of don't list it, but there are many sizes and sub-versions, and older bottles may differ. Read the label.
- **"Check the label"** means we couldn't confirm it confidently for every current version, so we won't guess.

## Alcohol-Free NyQuil: What's Different and What Isn't

Vicks makes NyQuil Alcohol Free Cold & Flu for people who want to skip the alcohol. Here's how it compares to the original:

- **Same purpose.** It's a night-time multi-symptom cold and flu liquid.
- **Same type of active ingredients.** Acetaminophen for pain and fever, dextromethorphan for cough, doxylamine for runny nose and sneezing (and drowsiness). Check the Drug Facts box for exact amounts on your version.
- **No alcohol as an inactive ingredient.** That's the difference.
- **Same warnings.** The label still tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks while using it, still carries the acetaminophen liver warning, and still warns about drowsiness when combined with alcohol, sedatives or tranquilizers.

If your goal is to avoid alcohol in the bottle, it's a good choice. If your goal is to take NyQuil after a night out, it doesn't solve the problem. Our [NyQuil and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol) covers the timing question in detail.

Another simple way to get NyQuil without alcohol is **NyQuil LiquiCaps**. The capsule form doesn't need alcohol to keep the ingredients dissolved. Some people also find capsules easier to dose accurately than a cup of syrup.

## Alcohol-Free Cough Syrup: What to Look For

The phrase "alcohol free cough syrup" covers a lot of products. A few practical tips:

- **Start with the front of the box.** Many brands print "alcohol free" (and often "sugar free" or "dye free") prominently because people look for it.
- **Confirm in the Drug Facts panel.** The last section, "Inactive ingredients," is where alcohol would appear. It may be listed as "alcohol" or "ethanol." Glycerin, propylene glycol and sorbitol are common solvents and sweeteners that are not drinking alcohol.
- **Match the active ingredient to your symptom.** A chesty, wet cough usually calls for an expectorant (guaifenesin), which thins mucus. A dry, tickly cough is what dextromethorphan is meant for. Multi-symptom products pile on extra drugs you may not need, which also means extra ways to interact with alcohol.
- **Watch out for "nighttime" or "PM" versions.** These almost always add a sedating antihistamine. Alcohol-free or not, that's the ingredient that clashes hardest with drinking.

For a deeper look at how each cough ingredient behaves with alcohol, including Robitussin and Mucinex versions, see our [cough medicine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol).

### A word on phenylephrine

Many daytime cold products, including DayQuil, have used **phenylephrine** as a decongestant. In 2023, an FDA advisory panel concluded that oral phenylephrine doesn't work as a nasal decongestant at the doses used in these products, and the FDA later proposed removing it from the list of approved oral decongestant ingredients. It isn't known to be dangerous with alcohol at label doses. It just may not be doing much for your stuffy nose. If congestion is your main problem, ask the pharmacist about alternatives (pseudoephedrine is kept behind the counter in the US; nasal sprays are another option).

## Alcohol-Free Sleep Aids: ZzzQuil and Benadryl

ZzzQuil is often confused with NyQuil, but it's a different product. It's a sleep aid with one active ingredient, diphenhydramine, and no cold medicines. The standard liquid is made without alcohol, and the LiquiCaps don't contain drinking alcohol either. Benadryl tablets and liqui-gels use the same active ingredient.

So if you want a sleep aid without alcohol in it, these fit. But diphenhydramine is exactly the ingredient that makes these risky after drinking. It's strongly sedating, it can cause next-day grogginess on its own, and alcohol amplifies all of that. It can also cause confusion, especially in older adults. Our [ZzzQuil and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/zzzquil-and-alcohol) and [Benadryl for hangover guide](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) go through the risks and how long to wait.

If your real problem is that you can't sleep after a night out, a sleep aid is usually the wrong fix. Alcohol itself disrupts the second half of the night, which is why you wake at 3 a.m. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on and what helps.

## Non-Drowsy and Lower-Risk Options If You've Had a Drink

Sometimes you're sick and you've also had a drink or two at dinner. No medicine is risk-free with alcohol, but some ingredients clash much less than others. Generally:

- **Saline nasal spray or rinse** contains no drugs at all. It's a reasonable first step for a stuffy nose on any night.
- **Plain guaifenesin** (plain Mucinex, plain Robitussin chest congestion) isn't strongly sedating. It's among the milder choices, though you should still keep drinking light.
- **Non-drowsy antihistamines** such as cetirizine (Zyrtec), loratadine (Claritin) and fexofenadine (Allegra) are much less sedating than diphenhydramine or doxylamine. Cetirizine can still cause some drowsiness in some people, and alcohol may add to it. See our [Zyrtec and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/zyrtec-and-alcohol).
- **Honey in warm water or tea** is a time-honored soother for a cough in adults and children over one year old. Never give honey to babies under 12 months.

What to skip on a drinking night: anything labeled nighttime, PM, sleep, or "nite," anything containing doxylamine or diphenhydramine, and stacking multiple acetaminophen products. If you're unsure, a pharmacist can look at your box and tell you in about thirty seconds.

## How Long to Wait Between Drinking and a Cold or Sleep Medicine

There's no official waiting period printed on these labels, and nobody can give you an exact number of hours that applies to everyone. What you can say with confidence:

- **Wait until you're fully sober** before taking anything sedating. The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot from person to person. After a heavy night, that can stretch well into the next day.
- **Going the other way, think about how long the medicine lasts.** Doxylamine and diphenhydramine can leave you drowsy for many hours, and extended-release products like Mucinex DM and Delsym are designed to last about 12 hours. If you took a night-time product, don't drink until the next day.
- **Count the acetaminophen.** If you took NyQuil or DayQuil and then want Tylenol for a headache, you're doubling up. Check the total against the label maximum.
- **If you drink 3 or more drinks most days,** ask a doctor or pharmacist before using any acetaminophen-containing product. That's what the label says.

## When to See a Doctor

Most colds clear up on their own in about a week to ten days. Medicines just make you more comfortable while that happens. Get medical advice rather than reaching for another bottle if:

- Your fever is high or lasts more than three days, or a cough lasts more than a week or comes back with fever, rash or a persistent headache. (Several cough medicine labels say to stop use and ask a doctor in these situations.)
- You're short of breath, wheezing, or have chest pain.
- You're coughing up blood, or thick discolored mucus with a high fever.
- Symptoms improve and then suddenly get worse.
- You have a long-term condition such as asthma, COPD, heart disease or diabetes and your cold is making it worse.

**Get emergency help (911 in the US) if** someone who mixed a cold or sleep medicine with alcohol can't be woken, has slow or irregular breathing, has bluish lips, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while very drowsy. Turn them on their side and stay with them. If you think someone took too much acetaminophen, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away, even if they seem fine, because early treatment works best.

## Smarter Ways to Get Through a Cold and a Night Out

If you're already sick, the simplest advice is also the most effective: skip the drinks until you're better. Alcohol dehydrates you, disrupts sleep, and won't help your immune system do its job. A cold plus a hangover is a miserable combination, and the medicines that help one tend to clash with the other.

If you do drink, keep it light, eat first, alternate with water, and don't plan on a NyQuil to knock you out afterward. Our [how to prevent a hangover guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, on nights they drink. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so treat it as promising rather than proven. To be clear about what it doesn't do: there is no good evidence that DHM makes it safe to combine alcohol with cold, cough or sleep medicines, and it doesn't replace any of the timing rules above. If you're curious, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple, budget-friendly option and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular combination formula. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and if you take any prescription medicine, our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) is worth a read before you start.

## The Bottom Line

- An alcohol-free NyQuil exists, and so do alcohol-free versions of most cough syrups. ZzzQuil, Benadryl, DayQuil and nearly all pills and capsules are made without drinking alcohol.
- The original NyQuil liquid lists alcohol at 10%, which works out to roughly a sixth of a standard drink per dose. That matters for people taking disulfiram or metronidazole, children, pregnancy, alcohol testing, and anyone avoiding alcohol entirely.
- **Alcohol-free doesn't mean safe with alcohol.** The sedating antihistamines (doxylamine, diphenhydramine), acetaminophen and dextromethorphan still interact with drinks in your system.
- On a drinking night, skip nighttime, PM and sleep products. Wait until you're sober, count your acetaminophen, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.
- Always confirm by reading the "Inactive ingredients" line on the box. Formulas change.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is there an alcohol-free NyQuil?**

Yes. Vicks sells NyQuil Alcohol Free Cold & Flu, a liquid with the same type of active ingredients as the original (acetaminophen, dextromethorphan and doxylamine) but without alcohol as an inactive ingredient. NyQuil LiquiCaps also don't contain drinking alcohol. Check the Drug Facts label on your box to confirm, since versions and formulas change.

**How much alcohol is in regular NyQuil?**

The original NyQuil Cold & Flu liquid lists alcohol at 10% as an inactive ingredient. A 30 mL adult dose therefore contains about 3 mL of alcohol, roughly 2.4 grams. A US standard drink has about 14 grams, so one dose is in the range of a sixth of a drink. It's a small amount, but it matters if you take disulfiram or metronidazole, are pregnant, are subject to alcohol testing, or avoid alcohol completely.

**Can I take alcohol-free NyQuil after drinking?**

It's not a good idea. Removing alcohol from the bottle doesn't change the active ingredients. Doxylamine is a sedating antihistamine that stacks with alcohol's sedation, and acetaminophen adds to your liver's workload. Wait until you're fully sober before taking any NyQuil, skip it entirely after a heavy night, and ask a doctor or pharmacist first if you drink 3 or more drinks a day.

**Does Robitussin have alcohol in it?**

Most current Robitussin cough liquids sold in the US are made without alcohol, and many are labeled that way. There are many versions, though, so check the "Inactive ingredients" line on your bottle. Separately from alcohol in the bottle, Robitussin DM and nighttime versions contain dextromethorphan or other ingredients that can add to drowsiness and dizziness if you've been drinking.

**Does ZzzQuil or Benadryl contain alcohol?**

The standard ZzzQuil liquid is made without alcohol, and ZzzQuil LiquiCaps and Benadryl tablets and liqui-gels don't use drinking alcohol in the formula. Children's Benadryl liquids are generally made without alcohol too. But both products contain diphenhydramine, a strong sedating antihistamine, so they shouldn't be combined with alcohol you've been drinking.

**Is DayQuil alcohol-free?**

Current US DayQuil Cold & Flu liquid and LiquiCaps are generally made without alcohol, but check the inactive ingredients on your package. DayQuil doesn't contain a sedating antihistamine, but it does contain acetaminophen, so the liver warning about 3 or more drinks a day still applies, and you shouldn't stack it with Tylenol or NyQuil.

**Can alcohol in cough syrup make me fail an alcohol test?**

A dose of a liquid medicine that contains alcohol, taken shortly before a breath test, could briefly register as mouth alcohol. Sensitive urine tests that look for alcohol breakdown products, such as EtG tests, can detect small exposures, and US federal guidance has flagged medicines and mouthwash as possible incidental sources. If you're subject to testing, choose an alcohol-free product and tell the tester what you've taken.

**What cold medicine is safest to take if I've had a drink?**

No cold medicine is completely risk-free with alcohol. Generally, saline nasal spray, plain guaifenesin and honey are among the mildest options, and non-drowsy antihistamines like loratadine or fexofenadine are far less sedating than nighttime formulas. Avoid anything labeled nighttime, PM or sleep, anything with doxylamine or diphenhydramine, and doubling up on acetaminophen. A pharmacist can check your specific product quickly.
